source.title: Generalization of Quantum Machine Learning Models Using Quantum Fisher Information Metric.

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper and supplemental material; no garbling or cutoff is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures generalization and its dependence on training data, ansatz, symmetry, and parameter count in quantum machine learning models, a new model setting for the catalog claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on quantum unitary learning and quantum classification, not classical networks fitting arbitrary labels on natural data. It does not test V1–V8 as stated. Its results concern same-task unitary learning, quantum training states, and symmetry-dependent in/out-of-distribution performance.
record.test_reason: The study reports quantum-circuit learning results, but none measures V1–V8. Increasing circuit parameters is not widening a classical network, DQFIM rank is not magnitude-aware sharpness, and the classification experiments use constructed quantum states rather than natural versus random labels. The record's T3 assignment is therefore incorrect.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate for the studied quantum models. The authors argue that DQFIM rank captures learnable degrees of freedom and characterizes training and generalization thresholds. Breaking data symmetry can reduce required training states, including for testing within a symmetry sector, but increases the required circuit parameter count. Their out-of-distribution advantage concerns these specific training and test distributions.
record.recipe_differences: Quantum variational unitary-learning and classification tasks; DQFIM rank and cost-function errors rather than classical-network label memorization or test accuracy.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported quantum generalization threshold changes with ansatz, training-data symmetry, and whether training data are product states or particle-number-conserving states; test distribution also changes the in/out-of-distribution comparison.

fits_no_version.finding: For the particle-number-conserving UXY circuit, product-state training requires two states for generalization, whereas training within the one-particle symmetry sector requires N states. Product-state training also generalizes to that symmetry sector with two states (Observations 3–4; Figures 3d and 8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the studied quantum unitary-learning task, breaking training-data symmetry can reduce sample requirements and allow out-of-distribution training to outperform training within the test distribution.

fits_no_version.finding: Training and test costs approach zero when circuit parameter count and training-state count exceed thresholds characterized by DQFIM rank; these thresholds depend on circuit and data structure (Figures 3, 5–11, 15–16).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: DQFIM rank characterizes parameter and sample thresholds for successful training and generalization in the studied quantum models.

fits_no_version.finding: Underparameterized quantum circuits can have a small training–test cost gap while both costs remain high (Supplement K; Figure 17).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A small empirical generalization gap can coexist with poor absolute test performance in underparameterized quantum learning models.

record.problems: The reported numerical results concern quantum models and unitary-learning costs, not the classical model and accuracy outcomes in the claim versions. Many findings are presented in figures; numerical summaries are generally stated in the text, but uncertainty is not consistently quantified. Some rank values are obtained by numerical extrapolation.
record.rows_left_out: No rows retained because the study does not measure the behavior named by any claim version. Quantum-model results are summarized under fits_no_version; the numerical outcomes do not directly measure any V1–V8 version.

untested.parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label held-out accuracy in the same architectures and training recipes.
Test error as network width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects on held-out classifier error across data sizes and regularization settings.
Magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation tolerance and its ranking of generalization gaps against other measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Retaining no version-linked rows is appropriate. The main-text numerical-results paragraph swaps the symmetric and non-symmetric descriptions of Wprod and Wp=1; Observations 3–4 and Supplements D–E consistently identify product states as non-symmetric and Wp=1 states as symmetric.

versions.untested_parts: Classical networks fitting random labels and generalizing on natural labels.
Width sweeps in one-hidden-layer ReLU networks on MNIST or downsampled CIFAR-10.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizers on image or language benchmarks.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout and weight-decay interventions on classifiers.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and other generalization measures in classical convolutional networks.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring test accuracy.
